set.definition: Destination where Caroline Beaufort was conducted after her father's death.
Hometown of Victor Frankenstein. Surrounded by a blue lake and snow-clad mountains. Republican city with simple, happy manners.
Native town of the creator. Surrounded by fields and the mountains of Jura.
Native city of the protagonist. Home of family members including Elizabeth and Ernest. Associated with a blue lake and rapid Rhône.
Destination of correspondence. Home of Mrs. Saville.
Native land of the letter writer. Source of southern gales.
A great monarchy surrounded by simpler republican institutions.
Native country of the narrator and destination of his return. Home and haven of friends and family.
A university town featuring a high white steeple. Home to professors of natural philosophy and chemistry.
A city in Europe featuring a church with a white steeple and clock. Location of a college.
Location of the narrator's former chamber where the monster's eyes were first seen.
Native country of the narrator. Home to piny mountains attended by distant white Alps. Features hills covered with vines, scattered cottages, and fair lakes reflecting a blue and gentle sky.
Large and luxurious city. Former home of the De Lacey family. Site of the imprisonment and trial of Safie's father.
Destination for shipping from Rotterdam.
Mountain with a bright summit. Features lightnings playing on its summit.
A beautiful snow-covered mountain. Surmounts all surrounding mountains.
Distant white mountains that crown the scenery of Switzerland.
A land of wonders sought for its pleasant climate.
Italian city. Port of refuge for the Turk and his daughter. Location where Felix and Safie spent time together.
A magnificent and sublime alpine valley. Bounded by high and snowy mountains. Features immense glaciers and avalanches.
A country visited by the narrator's parents.
A country of origin for the De Lacey family. Its government became enraged at the escape of a prisoner.
Mountains located near Bellerive. Source of a violent thunderstorm.
A destination on a post-road from St. Petersburgh. Mentioned in relation to a journey in Russia.
Location of a family campagne on the eastern shore of the lake. Setting for a violent and terrible thunderstorm.
City visited in Scotland. Known for its beauty, regularity of the new town, romantic castle, and delightful environs.
Historic city of ancient and picturesque colleges. Scene of pivotal events during the English Civil War. A place of beauty, towers, spires, and domes.
A river featured in the journey from Strasbourg to Rotterdam. Features a picturesque lower course with steep hills, ruined castles, and vineyards.
Meeting point for the journey. A stop along the Rhine river.
A raging river flowing among rocks in the ravine.
Mountainous region in England. Reminiscent of Swiss mountains with snow-covered northern slopes, lakes, and rocky streams.
A European country visited by the parents.
Detested shore. A place departed from by ship.
A steep hill bounding Plainpalais on the south. Features a nearly perpendicular ascent.
A destination in Scotland where a former visitor resided. Reached after passing through Coupar, St. Andrew's, and along the banks of the Tay.
A public walking area in Geneva. Bounded on the south by Mont Salêve. Scene of a tragic murder.
A major landmass mentioned in relation to a southern cape.
Region associated with a haram and traditional restrictions for female followers of Muhammad.
Native country of Safie. Destination for the Turkish merchant.
A continent mentioned in the context.
A destination for a wedding journey. A place with a spire shining under surrounding woods.
An ancient land. Mentioned in the context of being enslaved due to a lack of observed rules regarding domestic tranquillity and pursuits.
A town where the impoverished Beaufort retreated with his daughter. A place of wretchedness and unknown living conditions.
A town situated on the Rhine. Reached on the fifth day after departure from Strasbourg.
A blue sea of the south.
A city in Italy visited by the narrator's father.
A mountain summit accessed by a precipitous ascent. Overlooks a vast sea of ice. A place of sublime and majestic natural scenery.
A rapid river associated with early childhood memories. A beloved geographical feature of the narrator's homeland.
City along the Rhine. Destination for the boat journey from Strasbourg.
A region favorable for travelling by sledge over snow.
A valley passed through during the journey. Beautiful and picturesque. Features ruined castles and fertile fields.
Starting point of a voyage. City in Russia. Location where the narrator arrived before traveling to Archangel.
A country in the East. Destination for the Turk.
Region in the north. Visited by travellers for two months.

scenes.summary: Writing to his sister in England from Archangel, the narrator reflects on his preparations for his upcoming voyage, his lack of a sympathetic friend, and his new lieutenant.

The narrator details the noble background and character of his ship's master, who once gave up the woman he loved so she could marry another man, while confirming that his own voyage is delayed only until the spring weather allows embarkation.
Robert Walton writes a final letter expressing his mixed emotions of fear and excitement as he prepares to depart for unexplored regions.
R. W. writes a letter to his sister in England from a high northern latitude, reporting that he is safe, in good spirits, and sailing northward despite the presence of floating ice.

The ship becomes trapped in ice, where the crew spots a gigantic figure driving a sledge, and the next day rescues a freezing European man from a floating fragment of ice. After recovering, the stranger reveals he was pursuing the gigantic traveller across the ice to seek one who fled from him.

The narrator grows closer to the stranger on board his ship, eventually discussing his own polar enterprise. When the narrator speaks of sacrificing everything for knowledge, the stranger weeps and promises to tell his own tale as a warning.
The stranger agrees to tell his tale of past misfortunes to Walton, warning that the narrative will contain marvellous and harrowing occurrences, and Walton resolves to record the story in writing.

The narrator recounts his family background in Geneva, his father's friendship with a proud merchant named Beaufort who fell into poverty, and how his father tracked Beaufort to Lucerne only to find him dying in wretchedness while his daughter Caroline worked tirelessly to support them.
The narrator recounts his early childhood with his parents, their travels, and how they adopted Elizabeth Lavenza from an impoverished peasant family during a visit near the Lake of Como.
The narrator describes how Clerval pursued moral and adventurous ideals while Elizabeth served as a gentle, civilizing influence on both of them in their peaceful home.

The narrator reflects on his early childhood and recounts how finding a volume of Cornelius Agrippa at an inn near Thonon sparked his fateful interest in natural philosophy, despite his father dismissing the book as trash.

The narrator recounts his youthful fascination with ancient alchemical writers like Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus, followed by a transformative experience witnessing an oak tree destroyed by a violent thunderstorm near Bellerive, which temporarily turned his focus to electricity and mathematics.

Following the tragic death of the narrator's mother from scarlet fever, his departure for the university of Ingolstadt is finally realized. After a long journey, he arrives at his solitary apartment in the town.

The narrator arrives in Ingolstadt, meets the harsh professor Mr. Krempe who dismisses his alchemical studies, and later attends a lecture by M. Waldman which inspires him with a new zeal for modern science.

Following a sleepless night of inner turmoil, the narrator resolves to return to his studies and visits M. Waldman, who receives him kindly and encourages his pursuit of chemistry. Waldman advises him on the scope of natural philosophy, shows him his laboratory, and provides a list of recommended books, marking a turning point in the narrator's destiny.

Over two years at Ingolstadt, the narrator masters chemistry and natural philosophy under M. Krempe and M. Waldman, then turns to anatomy and the study of decay in charnel-houses until he discovers the secret of generating life and bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

The narrator recounts his months of obsessive, grueling labor spent gathering materials from charnel-houses and slaughterhouses to create and animate a gigantic human being, neglecting his friends, family, and health in the process.
scenes.setting_name: a solitary chamber, or rather cell, at the top of the house

scenes.summary: On a dreary November night at one in the morning, the narrator watches the lifeless creature he has labored to create finally open its dull yellow eye. Upon seeing it come to life, he is immediately struck with horror at the grotesque and hideous contrast of its features.

After fleeing his creation in terror and spending a wretched night wandering the streets of Ingolstadt, Frankenstein encounters his dear friend Henry Clerval arriving by the Swiss diligence and temporarily forgets his horror.

Victor returns to his room with Clerval, finds the monster gone, and immediately suffers a severe mental breakdown culminating in a months-long nervous fever. After recovering in the spring under Henry's devoted care, Victor is offered a letter from his cousin.
Clerval hands Victor a letter from Elizabeth, which provides family news, including the return of Justine Moritz after her mother's death and updates on Ernest and William.

Victor receives a letter from his father informing him that his youngest brother William has been murdered at Plainpalais, and that Elizabeth blames herself because a valuable miniature of Victor's mother was stolen from William.

Upon reading a letter from Alphonse Frankenstein detailing the murder of William, Frankenstein is struck with despair and resolves to return to Geneva immediately, departing after Clerval expresses his sympathy.

The narrator journeys back to Geneva and visits Plainpalais during a violent thunderstorm, where he encounters his gigantic creation and becomes convinced that it murdered William. He decides to keep his discovery a secret upon returning to his father's house.

Victor returns home after six years and learns from Ernest, his father, and Elizabeth that Justine Moritz has been accused of murdering William because his mother's picture was found in her pocket. Victor insists that Justine is innocent since he knows the true murderer, though he keeps the secret of his creation to himself.

The narrator attends Justine's trial, where overwhelming circumstantial evidence mounts against her, including her absence on the night of the murder and the discovery of the picture in her pocket. Justine offers a calm and logical defense explaining her whereabouts, but her witnesses hesitate and Elizabeth prepares to speak.

Elizabeth defends Justine at the trial, but Justine is condemned and allegedly confesses, leaving Victor in agony and Elizabeth heartbroken. Later, Elizabeth and Victor visit Justine in her cell, where Justine protests her innocence against the confession.

Justine explains to Elizabeth and the narrator why she falsely confessed, before she is ultimately executed on the morrow, leaving the narrator consumed by guilt and despair over both her death and William's.
Victor and his family retire to Bellerive, where Victor struggles with intense remorse and contemplates suicide while Elizabeth mourns the tragic death of Justine Moritz.

Overwhelmed by despair after Justine's death, the narrator leaves home and travels to the valley of Chamounix, finding temporary relief from his misery in the magnificent Alpine scenery before arriving exhausted at the village of Chamounix.

The narrator spends the day roaming through the valley and viewing the glacier of the Arveiron, finding that the sublime mountain scenery calms and consoles his grief. At night, he dreams peacefully of the grand shapes he witnessed during the day.

The narrator ascends Montanvert to seek solace in the majestic scenery, where he unexpectedly encounters his giant creation bounding across the glacier. Consumed by rage and horror, he confronts the monster, who demands that his creator listen to him or face the slaughter of the narrator's remaining friends.

Frankenstein confronts his creation with furious rage, but ultimately agrees to accompany him to a mountain hut and listen to his tale. Inside the hut, sitting by a fire, Frankenstein prepares to hear the creature's story.

The creature recounts his earliest memories following his animation, describing his confusion of senses, his escape into the forest near Ingolstadt, and his gradual learning to distinguish light, dark, food, and sounds.

The creature continues recounting his early life, describing how he discovered fire, learned to forage for food, left his initial habitation due to scarcity, encountered a terrified old man in a hut, and was later attacked and driven out of a village before taking refuge in a wretched hovel.
The creature settles into his refuge next to a cottage, where he observes a young girl, a young man, and an old blind man living together and experiences deep emotional stirrings.

The creature observes the daily routine of the cottagers, watching the young man and woman laboring around the cottage, sharing a meal, and listening to the old man play music and the youth read aloud.

The creature secretly observes the daily struggles, poverty, and emotional lives of Agatha and Felix, eventually learning to understand and speak their language while secretly aiding them with firewood and food.

The creature continues observing the cottagers through the winter and spring, learning language and secretly aiding Felix and Agatha with chores while grappling with horror at his own reflection. Encouraged by the changing season and the cottagers' improving circumstances, he nurtures high hopes of eventually revealing himself to them and winning their affection.

A mysterious young lady named Safie arrives at the cottage, bringing immense joy to Felix, Agatha, and the old man, while the creature uses her arrival and lessons to rapidly accelerate his own acquisition of their language over the following months.

The creature secretly continues observing the cottagers, learning language, human history, and social structures through Felix's lessons to Safie, which fills him with deep despair regarding his own monstrous isolation and lack of origin.
The creature relates the history of De Lacey, Agatha, and the Turkish merchant whose imprisonment brought ruin upon their family in Paris.

The creature recounts the history of Felix and Safie, explaining how Felix rescued Safie's father from prison, was subsequently betrayed by the ungrateful Turk after his family lost their fortune, and was ultimately reunited with Safie.

The creature recounts finding a leathern portmanteau containing books including Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and the Sorrows of Werther, which deeply influenced his developing intellect, emotions, and worldview.

The creature recounts how reading Paradise Lost and Victor's own journal deeply affected him, filling him with despair about his hideous appearance and solitary nature. He describes his careful preparations and hesitation before attempting to reveal himself to the cottagers.

The creature observes the changes in the cottage as Safie's presence brings happiness and plenty, contrasting his own growing misery and loneliness as autumn arrives. Despite his despair and reflections on his monstrous appearance, he yearns to reveal himself to the cottagers and win their kindness and sympathy.

The creature enters the cottage while only the blind old man is home and talks with him, hoping for his acceptance. However, when Felix, Safie, and Agatha return, Felix violently attacks the creature and drives him away.
The creature returns to the cottage only to find that Felix and the family have fled in terror, prompting him to burn the dwelling to the ground and set off toward Geneva to seek out his creator.

The creature recounts his long and difficult journey to Switzerland, where he saved a drowning girl only to be shot by a rustic, leading him to vow eternal hatred against mankind before finally arriving at the environs of Geneva.

The creature recounts how he encountered a young boy, learned he was a Frankenstein, strangled him to death in a fit of rage, stole a miniature portrait from his body, and framed a sleeping young woman by placing the portrait in her dress before finally demanding that his creator build him a female companion.

The creature demands that the narrator create a female companion for him, promising to live a harmless life in South America. Although initially filled with rage and horror, the narrator briefly feels compassion and considers the request before arguing against it and refusing.

After reflecting on the creature's arguments and recognizing his immense physical powers, the narrator agrees to create a female companion for him on the condition that he leaves Europe forever. The creature swears an oath to disappear permanently if this demand is granted and quickly departs down the mountain.

After spending the entire day listening to the creature's tale, the narrator descends the mountain in deep emotional turmoil and despair. Sitting at a resting-place by a fountain at night, he weepingly laments his miserable thoughts and the weight of the surrounding elements.

The narrator travels back through Chamounix and returns home to Geneva, where his distressed appearance alarms his family. Overwhelmed by silence and a sense of isolation, he resolves to undertake a detested task in order to save them.

Upon returning to Geneva, the narrator procrastinates on building the female creature while trying to recover his health and spirits through boat rides on the lake, until his father approaches him with a suspicion regarding his ongoing unhappiness.

Victor's father proposes an immediate marriage between Victor and Elizabeth, but Victor feels horror and dismay at the idea because he is still bound to fulfill his promise to create a mate for the monster.

The narrator resolves to travel to England to secretly fulfill his monstrous task, convincing his father and setting off with chemical instruments. After arriving in Strasbourg, he meets Clerval, whose joy and appreciation of nature contrast sharply with the narrator's inner misery.
The travelers journey down the Rhine in a boat from Strasbourg toward Rotterdam, passing islands, towns, and picturesque landscapes before arriving at Mayence.

The narrator recalls traveling down the Rhine with Henry, who marveled at the picturesque scenery and expressed his deep love for nature. Reflecting on Henry's untimely death and noble character, the narrator pauses in sorrow before continuing his tale.
The narrator and his companion travel from Cologne through Holland and Rotterdam to finally arrive in England, sailing up the Thames to London.
scenes.setting_name: Holland, Rotterdam, England, the Thames, London

scenes.summary: While staying in London, the narrator seeks information to fulfill his promise while Clerval pursues his own ambitions regarding India. After several months, they receive an invitation from a former visitor in Geneva to travel north to Perth in Scotland, which Clerval eagerly accepts and the narrator views as an opportunity to see natural scenery.
The narrator and his companions depart London at the end of March, traveling through Windsor and Oxford before planning further northward journeys toward Scotland.

Victor and Henry travel through England and Scotland, visiting places like Oxford, Matlock, Cumberland, Westmorland, and Edinburgh, before Victor decides to separate from Henry in Perth and isolate himself in a remote hut in the Orkneys to carry out his dark task.
The narrator reflects on the grim solitude and horrifying nature of his work while laboring on his new creation, haunted by constant dread and fear of his persecutor.

The narrator sits in his laboratory reflecting on the terrifying consequences of creating a female companion, ultimately destroying his work when he sees the daemon watching him through the casement. Hours later, after locking himself in his room, he hears someone land in a boat close to his house.

The creature confronts the narrator in his room, demanding to know why his work was destroyed and threatening him with relentless revenge. The narrator remains firm in his refusal to create a companion.

After a fierce exchange, the creature departs by boat while vowing to be with the narrator on his wedding night. Left alone, the narrator suffers through a night of intense agitation and despair on the island before finding some composure after sleep.

Victor receives a letter from Clerval asking him to meet in Perth, destroys his laboratory remains, and dumps them at sea. While sailing afterwards, a storm blows him off course into an unknown English-speaking town.

Upon landing in a small Irish town, the narrator is treated with hostility by a gathering crowd and led away by an ill-looking man to meet Mr. Kirwin, a magistrate, in order to give an account of the death of a murdered gentleman found the previous night.

The narrator is brought before a magistrate who hears witness depositions detailing the discovery of a murdered young man on the beach and circumstantial evidence linking the narrator's boat to the crime scene.

The narrator is taken to view the body of Henry Clerval and collapses in convulsions, followed by a severe two-month fever in prison during which Mr. Kirwin kindly provides care. Upon recovering his senses in a dungeon, the narrator receives a visit from Mr. Kirwin, who expresses sympathy for his miserable state.
Mr. Kirwin discusses the narrator's situation and reveals that a friend has come to visit him, prompting the narrator to panic and beg for the visitor to be kept away.

The magistrate informs the narrator that his father has come to visit him in prison, instantly transforming the narrator's despair into joy. His father enters, reassures him of the safety of Elizabeth and Ernest, but then touches upon the tragic death of Clerval, plunging the narrator back into grief.

The narrator is freed from prison after the grand jury rejects the bill against him, and he sets sail for Geneva with his father, battling deep melancholy, suicidal impulses, and terrifying nightmares.
Upon arriving in Paris, the narrator suffers from overwhelming guilt over the deaths of William, Justine, and Henry, confessing his responsibility to his father.

Victor reflects on his inability to explain his guilt to his father, who remains convinced that Victor's confessions are the result of madness. Over time, Victor learns to master his outward grief and maintains silence regarding the creature he created.

While in Paris, the narrator receives a letter from Elizabeth expressing concern about his well-being, mentioning her conversation with his uncle, and hinting at a need for an explanation before they meet.
Elizabeth Lavenza writes a letter to Victor in Geneva, assuring him that she desires his happiness above all and releases him from any obligation to marry her if his heart lies elsewhere.
The narrator reflects on the creature's menacing vow to be with him on his wedding night, anticipating a deadly struggle that will either end his suffering or leave him utterly desolate.
The narrator reads a letter from Elizabeth and resolves not to delay their wedding despite the monster's threats of violence on his wedding night.

The narrator writes a calm letter to Elizabeth promising to reveal a dreadful secret after their wedding, and shortly after, they return to Geneva where Elizabeth attempts to soothe his recurring bouts of madness and remorse.

Victor agrees to marry Elizabeth in ten days, fatalistically accepting the monster's threat while hiding his dread behind apparent cheerfulness. Preparations are made, and it is agreed they will spend their first days at Villa Lavenza near Como.
Victor and Elizabeth marry, and they travel by water to Evian for their wedding night while Victor dreads the monster's promised attack.

Victor and Elizabeth arrive at an inn during a storm, where Victor anxiously guards against an expected attack by his adversary. After convincing Elizabeth to retire to her room, Victor hears a dreadful scream and discovers that Elizabeth has been murdered by the creature.

After discovering the murdered body of Elizabeth and catching a brief glimpse of the monster escaping into the lake, the narrator travels back to Geneva, where his father dies of grief and he himself is confined to a madhouse. Upon his release, he vows revenge and reports the murderer to a magistrate.
The narrator recounts his history and accuses his destroyer before a magistrate, who ultimately doubts the tale and treats him as if deranged, prompting the narrator to leave in anger.
Consumed by fury and a desire for revenge, the narrator leaves Geneva and begins years of wandering, eventually returning to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth, and his father are buried.
The narrator swears a solemn and vengeful oath at the cemetery to pursue and destroy the daemon responsible for the death of his friends and family.

The narrator hears the fiend's laughter in the night, catches a brief glimpse of him in the moonlight, and embarks on a prolonged pursuit following him down the Rhône to the Mediterranean and toward the Black Sea.
The narrator recounts his long pursuit of the daemon across the wilds of Tartary and Russia, sustained by unexpected signs and assistance along the way.

The narrator continues his relentless pursuit of the creature across increasingly freezing and desolate northern landscapes, sustained by his dreams and fueled by the taunting inscriptions left by his foe.
The narrator learns from villagers that the fiend crossed the sea in a sledge, and despite despair, he sets out across the Frozen Ocean in pursuit.
The narrator chases his enemy across the ice on a sledge, nearly reaching him before the ice splits apart during a violent ground sea, leaving the narrator drifting on a shrinking piece of ice.
The rescued stranger recounts his perilous journey on the ice-raft chasing his enemy and begs Walton to swear that he will hunt down and kill the creature if he dies.
The narrator reflects on a week spent listening to his guest's extraordinary tale and admiring his immense intellect, eloquence, and past greatness.

The stranger reflects on his past ambition, his creation of a living being, and his tragic fall into despair. The narrator laments the potential loss of this newly found friend whom he has grown to admire.
Walton writes to Margaret from a ship surrounded by dangerous ice in the Arctic, noting that his guest's eloquence has temporarily raised the desperate sailors' spirits.

Mutinous sailors demand that the ship return south, but Frankenstein rouses them with a speech before relapsing into severe illness. Days later, as the ice clears and the ship begins its return to England, a dying Frankenstein urges the narrator to continue the task of destroying his enemy.

Frankenstein dies aboard the ship, leaving Walton to grieve and write to Margaret as midnight approaches. Suddenly, a strange hoarser voice is heard coming from the cabin where Frankenstein's remains lie.

The narrator enters the cabin to find the gigantic and hideous creature weeping over the dead body of Frankenstein. Upon being discovered, the creature pauses briefly before staring at the corpse in a fit of uncontrollable rage.

The creature laments over the corpse of Frankenstein, expressing remorse and explaining the inner torment that drove him to commit his crimes. The narrator, initially moved, grows indignant again and accuses the creature of hypocrisy.

The creature laments his crimes and misery over the body of Frankenstein, then declares his intention to travel to the northern extremity of the globe and destroy himself on a funeral pile before leaping out of the cabin-window onto an ice-raft.

threads.question: Will R. Walton succeed in his dangerous voyage to discover a passage near the pole?
threads.raise_quote: If I succeed, many, many months, perhaps years, will pass before you and I may meet.

answers.text: The voyage is delayed due to the severe winter, but the narrator expects to sail soon as the spring promises an early season.
answers.quote: The winter has been dreadfully severe; but the spring promises well, and it is considered as a remarkably early season; so that perhaps I may sail sooner than I expected.

answers.text: The expedition has reached a very high latitude in good spirits and with a firm crew.
answers.quote: We have already reached a very high latitude; but it is the height of summer, and although not so warm as in England, the southern gales, which blow us speedily towards those shores which I so ardently desire to attain, breathe a degree of renovating warmth which I had not expected.

answers.text: The voyage has been temporarily delayed by ice entrapment, but the ship has now been freed and continues north.
answers.quote: before night the ice broke, and freed our ship.

answers.text: The stranger believes the narrator's polar expedition is a dangerous madness akin to his own.
answers.quote: Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you drank also of the intoxicating draught?

answers.text: The stranger warns Walton that his pursuit of knowledge may act like a serpent and bring disaster.
answers.quote: You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting you, as mine has been.

threads.question: Who is the lieutenant that the narrator has hired for his enterprise?
threads.raise_quote: My lieutenant, for instance, is a man of wonderful courage and enterprise; he is madly desirous of glory

threads.question: Who is the mysterious European rescued from the ice?
threads.raise_quote: It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before, which had drifted towards us in the night, on a large fragment of ice.

answers.text: He is a European who is pursuing a giant across the ice.
answers.quote: It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before, which had drifted towards us in the night, on a large fragment of ice.

threads.question: Why is the stranger pursuing the giant he calls a daemon?
threads.raise_quote: To seek one who fled from me.

threads.question: What is the stranger's tragic story that will cause the narrator to dash his cup from his lips?
threads.raise_quote: Hear me⁠—let me reveal my tale, and you will dash the cup from your lips!

answers.text: The stranger begins his tragic story with his family background in Geneva and his father's friendship with Beaufort.
answers.quote: I am by birth a Genevese; and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic.

answers.text: The stranger's story begins with an account of his harmonious childhood, affectionate parents, and his early relationship with Elizabeth Lavenza.
answers.quote: Everyone loved Elizabeth. The passionate and almost reverential attachment with which all regarded her became, while I shared it, my pride and my delight.

answers.text: The stranger's childhood was blessed by the gentle and refining presence of Elizabeth.
answers.quote: The saintly soul of Elizabeth shone like a shrine-dedicated lamp in our peaceful home.

answers.text: The stranger's tragic story continues with his early introduction to natural philosophy through the works of Cornelius Agrippa.
answers.quote: Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate; I desire, therefore, in this narration, to state those facts which led to my predilection for that science.

answers.text: The stranger's tragic story continues with his return to ancient studies and his mentorship under M. Waldman in chemistry.
answers.quote: There only remained a resolution to return to my ancient studies, and to devote myself to a science for which I believed myself to possess a natural talent.

answers.text: The stranger's tragic story continues with his obsessive creation of an eight-foot-tall artificial man in a secret cell.
answers.quote: It was with these feelings that I began the creation of a human being. As the minuteness of the parts formed a great hindrance to my speed, I resolved, contrary to my first intention, to make the being of a gigantic stature

threads.question: What are the unparalleled misfortunes and marvellous occurrences that the stranger is about to relate?
threads.raise_quote: Prepare to hear of occurrences which are usually deemed marvellous.

answers.text: They involve a disastrous course that mirrors Walton's dangerous pursuit of knowledge.
answers.quote: Prepare to hear of occurrences which are usually deemed marvellous.

answers.text: The unparalleled misfortunes and marvellous occurrences begin with the history of his father and Beaufort's daughter.
answers.quote: As the circumstances of his marriage illustrate his character, I cannot refrain from relating them.

answers.text: The stranger recounts his serene early life and the adoption of Elizabeth as part of his background.
answers.quote: Elizabeth Lavenza became the inmate of my parents’ house⁠—my more than sister⁠—the beautiful and adored companion of all my occupations and my pleasures.

answers.text: The narrator traces his marvelous occurrences and misfortunes back to a childhood discovery of Cornelius Agrippa's works.
answers.quote: I find it arise, like a mountain river, from ignoble and almost forgotten sources; but, swelling as it proceeded, it became the torrent which, in its course, has swept away all my hopes and joys.

answers.text: The narrator continues recounting his marvelous occurrences by detailing his arrival in Ingolstadt and his fateful encounters with his professors.
answers.quote: Such were my reflections during the first two or three days of my residence at Ingolstadt, which were chiefly spent in becoming acquainted with the localities, and the principal residents in my new abode.

answers.text: The marvelous occurrences and misfortunes stem from his pivotal decision to become M. Waldman's disciple in chemistry.
answers.quote: Thus ended a day memorable to me: it decided my future destiny.

answers.text: The marvelous occurrences stem from his scientific breakthroughs and his discovery of how to bestow animation upon lifeless matter.
answers.quote: I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life; nay, more, I became myself capable of bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

threads.question: What happened to Elizabeth Lavenza's biological father in the dungeons of Austria?
threads.raise_quote: Whether he had died, or still lingered in the dungeons of Austria, was not known.

answers.text: It is unknown whether he died or is still imprisoned.
answers.quote: Whether he had died, or still lingered in the dungeons of Austria, was not known.

threads.question: What are the specific contents of the volume of Cornelius Agrippa that so thoroughly captivated the narrator's imagination?
threads.raise_quote: the theory which he attempts to demonstrate, and the wonderful facts which he relates, soon changed this feeling into enthusiasm.

answers.text: The book contains theories and wonderful facts concerning natural philosophy that inspired the narrator.
answers.quote: the theory which he attempts to demonstrate, and the wonderful facts which he relates, soon changed this feeling into enthusiasm.

threads.question: What kind of lectures will M. Waldman deliver, and how will they shape the narrator's future?
threads.raise_quote: So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein⁠—more, far more, will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

answers.text: M. Waldman's lecture inspires the narrator to pioneer a new way and explore unknown powers.
answers.quote: So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein⁠—more, far more, will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

threads.question: What specific books and branches of natural philosophy will M. Waldman recommend to the narrator?
threads.raise_quote: I requested his advice concerning the books I ought to procure.

answers.text: He advised applying to every branch of natural philosophy including mathematics and provided a list of books.
answers.quote: I requested his advice concerning the books I ought to procure.

threads.question: What is the astonishing secret and cause of generation and life that the narrator discovered?
threads.raise_quote: I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life; nay, more, I became myself capable of bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

answers.text: It is a chemical and physiological method discovered through studying the decay of the human body in charnel-houses.
answers.quote: I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life; nay, more, I became myself capable of bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

threads.question: What will happen when the narrator's gigantic creation is finally animated?
threads.raise_quote: every day showed me more plainly how well I had succeeded. But my enthusiasm was checked by my anxiety, and I appeared rather like one doomed by slavery to toil in the mines

answers.text: The narrator believes his creation will be successful and that he will then rest and regain his health.
answers.quote: every day showed me more plainly how well I had succeeded. But my enthusiasm was checked by my anxiety, and I appeared rather like one doomed by slavery to toil in the mines

answers.text: The creation is successfully animated, but it proves to be a hideous monster that fills its creator with horror rather than joy.
answers.quote: His yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath; his hair was of a lustrous black, and flowing; his teeth of a pearly whiteness; but these luxuriances only formed a more horrid contrast with his watery eyes

answers.text: The gigantic creation has fled the apartment upon animation, leaving Victor to suffer a nervous breakdown.
answers.quote: I became assured that my enemy had indeed fled

answers.text: William has been murdered, sending the narrator into deep despair.
answers.quote: Tears also gushed from the eyes of Clerval, as he read the account of my misfortune.

answers.text: The gigantic creation has committed its first known crime by murdering William in Geneva.
answers.quote: He was the murderer! I could not doubt it.

threads.question: Why did Henry Clerval come to Ingolstadt?
threads.raise_quote: and his own good fortune in being permitted to come to Ingolstadt.

answers.text: He has been permitted by his father to undertake a voyage of discovery to learn things beyond bookkeeping.
answers.quote: and his own good fortune in being permitted to come to Ingolstadt.

threads.question: What will Elizabeth's letter reveal to Victor?
threads.raise_quote: If this is your present temper, my friend, you will perhaps be glad to see a letter that has been lying here some days for you: it is from your cousin, I believe.

answers.text: It is a letter inquiring about his long silence and expressing the family's unease.
answers.quote: If this is your present temper, my friend, you will perhaps be glad to see a letter that has been lying here some days for you: it is from your cousin, I believe.

closed.answer: Elizabeth's letter reveals news of Victor's family, the health of his father and brothers, and the return of Justine Moritz to their household.
closed.quote: Little alteration, except the growth of our dear children, has taken place since you left us.

threads.question: Who murdered William and stole the miniature?

answers.text: The creature framed Justine for the murder of William.
answers.quote: Could the daemon, who had (I did not for a minute doubt) murdered my brother, also in his hellish sport have betrayed the innocent to death and ignominy?

answers.text: Victor's created daemon murdered William.
Justine has been executed for a murder she did not commit, while the true killer remains unpunished.
answers.quote: And on the morrow Justine died.

answers.text: Justine has been wrongfully executed for William's murder.
The creature confesses to murdering William.
The creature stole William's miniature portrait and framed a sleeping woman.
answers.quote: As I fixed my eyes on the child, I saw something glittering on his breast. I took it; it was a portrait of a most lovely woman.

closed.answer: The creature murdered William and stole the miniature.
closed.quote: I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.

threads.question: How will the narrator respond to the realization that his creation is a murderer while keeping it a secret?
threads.raise_quote: These reflections determined me, and I resolved to remain silent.

answers.text: He will hide his knowledge and suffer in silence to avoid being thought insane.
answers.quote: These reflections determined me, and I resolved to remain silent.

answers.text: He will keep his secret and suffer internal torment rather than confess.
answers.quote: Anguish and despair had penetrated into the core of my heart; I bore a hell within me, which nothing could extinguish.

answers.text: He continues to conceal his secret and suffers internal torment, fearing new crimes.
answers.quote: I had an obscure feeling that all was not over, and that he would still commit some signal crime, which by its enormity should almost efface the recollection of the past.

answers.text: The narrator confronts his creation openly for the first time since abandoning him, leading to a direct confrontation.

threads.question: How did the picture of Victor's mother end up in Justine's pocket?
threads.raise_quote: one of the servants, happening to examine the apparel she had worn on the night of the murder, had discovered in her pocket the picture of my mother

threads.question: Will Justine be convicted and suffer execution at her trial today?
threads.raise_quote: But she will be tried today, and you will then hear all.

answers.text: Her family hopes she will be acquitted, but the circumstantial evidence weighs heavily against her.
answers.quote: But she will be tried today, and you will then hear all.

answers.text: Justine's conviction and execution appear nearly certain because the incriminating evidence cannot be explained away by her or her witnesses.
answers.quote: Elizabeth saw even this last resource, her excellent dispositions and irreproachable conduct, about to fail the accused

answers.text: Justine was convicted at her trial and condemned to death.
answers.quote: The ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

closed.answer: Justine was convicted and condemned at her trial.
closed.quote: The ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

threads.question: Why did Justine falsely confess to the murder?
threads.raise_quote: The person to whom I addressed myself added, that Justine had already confessed her guilt.

threads.question: Will the narrator ever confess his secret and reveal the true murderer of William and destroyer of Justine?
threads.raise_quote: Thus I might proclaim myself a madman, but not revoke the sentence passed upon my wretched victim.

answers.text: He is too cowardly and afraid of being thought mad to confess.
answers.quote: Thus I might proclaim myself a madman, but not revoke the sentence passed upon my wretched victim.

answers.text: He remains overwhelmed by agony and guilt, keeping his secret hidden even as Elizabeth pleads with him to calm himself.
answers.quote: I listened to this discourse with the extremest agony. I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer.

threads.question: Will Victor ultimately seek revenge and attempt to kill the monster he created?
threads.raise_quote: I wished to see him again, that I might wreak the utmost extent of abhorrence on his head, and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

answers.text: He desperately wishes to hunt down and destroy the creature.
answers.quote: I wished to see him again, that I might wreak the utmost extent of abhorrence on his head, and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

answers.text: Victor encounters the monster face-to-face on the glacier and resolves to kill him in mortal combat.
answers.quote: I trembled with rage and horror, resolving to wait his approach, and then close with him in mortal combat.

answers.text: Victor's immediate attempt to destroy his creation fails as the creature easily eludes him and persuades him to listen instead.

threads.question: What conditions does the creature want the narrator to comply with?
threads.raise_quote: If you will comply with my conditions, I will leave them and you at peace; but if you refuse, I will glut the maw of death, until it be satiated with the blood of your remaining friends.

answers.text: The creature demands that the narrator fulfill his duties as a creator towards him.
answers.quote: If you will comply with my conditions, I will leave them and you at peace; but if you refuse, I will glut the maw of death, until it be satiated with the blood of your remaining friends.

answers.text: The creature demands that Victor create a female companion of the same species.
answers.quote: My companion must be of the same species, and have the same defects. This being you must create.

answers.text: The creature elaborates that he and his companion will retire to the wilds of South America and live harmlessly on a vegetarian diet.
answers.quote: I will go to the vast wilds of South America. My food is not that of man; I do not destroy the lamb and the kid to glut my appetite; acorns and berries afford me sufficient nourishment.

threads.question: What is the creature's tale and how will it explain his actions?
threads.raise_quote: Listen to my tale: when you have heard that, abandon or commiserate me, as you shall judge that I deserve. But hear me.

answers.text: The creature's tale begins with his confused awakening, sensory overload, and flight into the forest near Ingolstadt.
answers.quote: A strange multiplicity of sensations seized me, and I saw, felt, heard, and smelt, at the same time

answers.text: The creature's tale describes his early experiences with fire, food scarcity, and hostile human encounters after fleeing his creator.
answers.quote: One of the best of these I entered; but I had hardly placed my foot within the door, before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted.

answers.text: The creature takes refuge next to a cottage and begins observing a family of cottagers, learning about human affection and sorrow.
answers.quote: The silver hair and benevolent countenance of the aged cottager won my reverence, while the gentle manners of the girl enticed my love.

answers.text: The creature spends his time secretly observing the daily lives and domestic habits of the cottagers.
answers.quote: In the evening, the young girl and her companion were employed in various occupations which I did not understand

answers.text: The creature learns to speak by observing the cottagers, secretly helps them with their chores, and plans to introduce himself once he masters their language.
answers.quote: I ought not to make the attempt until I had first become master of their language; which knowledge might enable me to make them overlook the deformity of my figure

answers.text: The creature continues detailing his education and the emotional turmoil it caused him before his encounter with the cottagers.
answers.quote: I will soon explain to what these feelings tended

answers.text: The creature recounts the backstory and ruin of De Lacey and his family.
The creature tells the detailed background story of Felix, De Lacey, Agatha, and Safie to explain their impoverished state.
answers.quote: Such were the events that preyed on the heart of Felix, and rendered him, when I first saw him, the most miserable of his family.

answers.text: The creature's tale concludes its account of the cottagers with their abandonment of the home following the violent confrontation.
answers.quote: I never saw any of the family of De Lacey more.

answers.text: The creature's early attempts at benevolence were violently rejected by humans, sealing his turn toward malice.
answers.quote: Inflamed by pain, I vowed eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind.

threads.question: Will the creature's tale prove that he is indeed the murderer of Victor's brother?
threads.raise_quote: I had hitherto supposed him to be the murderer of my brother, and I eagerly sought a confirmation or denial of this opinion.

answers.text: The creature confesses to murdering Victor's younger brother.
answers.quote: I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.

closed.quote: I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.

threads.question: Whose hut did the creature enter, and why did the old man flee in terror?
threads.raise_quote: An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast. He turned on hearing a noise; and, perceiving me, shrieked loudly, and, quitting the hut, ran across the fields with a speed of which his debilitated form hardly appeared capable.

answers.text: The old man fled because he was terrified by the creature's unusual and frightening appearance.
answers.quote: An old man sat in it, near a fire, over which he was preparing his breakfast. He turned on hearing a noise; and, perceiving me, shrieked loudly, and, quitting the hut, ran across the fields with a speed of which his debilitated form hardly appeared capable.

threads.question: Why do all the villagers react with immediate violence and terror upon seeing the creature?
threads.raise_quote: One of the best of these I entered; but I had hardly placed my foot within the door, before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country

answers.text: His monstrous and unnatural appearance causes immediate panic and hostility in human settlements.
answers.quote: One of the best of these I entered; but I had hardly placed my foot within the door, before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted. The whole village was roused; some fled, some attacked me, until, grievously bruised by stones and many other kinds of missile weapons, I escaped to the open country

threads.question: Who are the inhabitants of the cottage and what is their history?
threads.raise_quote: In one corner, near a small fire, sat an old man, leaning his head on his hands in a disconsolate attitude.

answers.text: They are a poor, gentle family consisting of an old blind man, a young girl, and a young man.
answers.quote: In one corner, near a small fire, sat an old man, leaning his head on his hands in a disconsolate attitude.

threads.question: What is the relationship between the old man, the young man, and the girl?
threads.raise_quote: The old man had, in the meantime, been pensive; but, on the appearance of his companions, he assumed a more cheerful air, and they sat down to eat.

threads.question: Why does the young man express such deep sadness despite their peaceful life?
threads.raise_quote: yet his eyes and attitude expressed the utmost sadness and despondency.

threads.question: What is the cause of the cottagers' poverty and frequent unhappiness?
threads.raise_quote: A considerable period elapsed before I discovered one of the causes of the uneasiness of this amiable family: it was poverty; and they suffered that evil in a very distressing degree.

answers.text: Their poverty and the difficulty of procuring food during winter caused their distress.
answers.quote: A considerable period elapsed before I discovered one of the causes of the uneasiness of this amiable family: it was poverty; and they suffered that evil in a very distressing degree.

threads.question: Will the creature successfully learn to speak and interact with the cottagers?
threads.raise_quote: This was indeed a godlike science, and I ardently desired to become acquainted with it.

answers.text: He learns the names of familiar objects and the names of the cottagers over the course of the winter.
answers.quote: This was indeed a godlike science, and I ardently desired to become acquainted with it.

answers.text: The creature successfully learns most of the cottagers' language within two months alongside Safie.
answers.quote: Safie was always gay and happy; she and I improved rapidly in the knowledge of language, so that in two months I began to comprehend most of the words uttered by my protectors.

answers.text: The creature successfully masters language, reading, and human history by observing the lessons given to Safie.
answers.quote: whilst I comprehended and could imitate almost every word that was spoken.

answers.text: The creature deliberately delays his planned encounter with the cottagers out of fear and a desire to further improve his understanding.
answers.quote: I postponed this attempt for some months longer; for the importance attached to its success inspired me with a dread lest I should fail.

answers.text: The creature's attempt to interact with the cottagers ends permanently when they abandon the cottage in terror.
answers.quote: I never saw any of the family of De Lacey more.

closed.answer: The creature's interactions with the cottagers fail completely, resulting in their flight and the destruction of their home.
closed.quote: I never saw any of the family of De Lacey more.

threads.question: How will the cottagers actually react when they finally discover the creature?
threads.raise_quote: I imagined that they would be disgusted, until, by my gentle demeanour and conciliating words, I should first win their favour, and afterwards their love.

answers.text: He believes they will initially be disgusted by his appearance but will eventually accept him due to his gentle demeanor.
answers.quote: I imagined that they would be disgusted, until, by my gentle demeanour and conciliating words, I should first win their favour, and afterwards their love.

answers.text: The creature desperately wants to approach the cottagers to gain their affection, though he deeply fears they will reject him with disdain and horror.
answers.quote: I dared not think that they would turn them from me with disdain and horror.

answers.text: The cottagers react with immediate horror, fainting, fleeing, and violently attacking the creature.
answers.quote: Agatha fainted; and Safie, unable to attend to her friend, rushed out of the cottage. Felix darted forward, and with supernatural force tore me from his father, to whose knees I clung: in a transport of fury, he dashed me to the ground, and struck me violently with a stick.

closed.answer: The cottagers reject the creature with complete revulsion and violence upon discovering him.
closed.quote: Felix darted forward, and with supernatural force tore me from his father, to whose knees I clung: in a transport of fury, he dashed me to the ground, and struck me violently with a stick.

threads.question: Who is Safie and why has she traveled to find Felix?
threads.raise_quote: It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman as a guide.

answers.text: She is a foreign visitor referred to as the sweet Arabian whom Felix loves.
answers.quote: It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman as a guide.

answers.text: Safie is the daughter of a Turkish merchant imprisoned in Paris.
answers.quote: The father of Safie had been the cause of their ruin. He was a Turkish merchant, and had inhabited Paris for many years

answers.text: Safie fled her father's home in Italy and traveled alone through Germany to find Felix.
answers.quote: Taking with her some jewels that belonged to her, and a sum of money, she quitted Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn, but who understood the common language of Turkey, and departed for Germany.

threads.question: What is the creature's true origin and who is his creator?
threads.raise_quote: Of my creation and creator I was absolutely ignorant

answers.text: He remains entirely ignorant of how he was created.
answers.quote: Of my creation and creator I was absolutely ignorant

answers.text: He continues to ponder his unknown origin and monstrous nature while educating himself.
answers.quote: These questions continually recurred, but I was unable to solve them.

answers.text: The creature discovers Victor's laboratory journal in the pockets of the clothes he took, learning the full details of his own creation.
answers.quote: It was your journal of the four months that preceded my creation. You minutely described in these papers every step you took in the progress of your work

threads.question: Why did the father of Safie become obnoxious to the French government?
threads.raise_quote: He was a Turkish merchant, and had inhabited Paris for many years, when, for some reason which I could not learn, he became obnoxious to the government.

threads.question: Will Safie be able to defy her father and reunite with Felix?
threads.raise_quote: When the news reached Leghorn, that Felix was deprived of his wealth and rank, the merchant commanded his daughter to think no more of her lover, but to prepare to return to her native country.

threads.question: How did the portmanteau containing the books end up in the wood?
threads.raise_quote: I found on the ground a leathern portmanteau, containing several articles of dress and some books.

threads.question: How will Victor Frankenstein react when his creation finally arrives in Geneva to confront him?
threads.raise_quote: You had mentioned Geneva as the name of your native town; and towards this place I resolved to proceed.

threads.question: What will Victor do in response to the creature's demand for a female companion?
threads.raise_quote: This being you must create.

answers.text: Victor initially refuses outright, but his resolve weakens into hesitation as the creature argues his case.
answers.quote: I was moved. I shuddered when I thought of the possible consequences of my consent; but I felt that there was some justice in his argument.

answers.text: Victor agrees to build a female companion on the condition that the creature quits Europe forever.
answers.quote: I consent to your demand, on your solemn oath to quit Europe forever, and every other place in the neighbourhood of man, as soon as I shall deliver into your hands a female who will accompany you in your exile.

answers.text: Victor begins his long descent from the mountain after hearing the creature's full tale, weighed down by dark emotions.
answers.quote: occupied as I was by the emotions which the occurrences of the day had produced.

answers.text: Victor decides to comply with the creature's demand in order to save his family.
answers.quote: and to save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most abhorred task.

answers.text: Victor resolves to fulfill his promise to create a female companion before marrying Elizabeth.
answers.quote: I must perform my engagement, and let the monster depart with his mate, before I allowed myself to enjoy the delight of an union from which I expected peace.

answers.text: Victor decides to travel to England under the guise of pleasure to secretly build the female companion.
answers.quote: I remembered only, and it was with a bitter anguish that I reflected on it, to order that my chemical instruments should be packed to go with me.

answers.text: Victor is actively collecting the materials necessary for his new creation while staying in London.
answers.quote: I now also began to collect the materials necessary for my new creation, and this was to me like the torture of single drops of water continually falling on the head.

answers.text: Victor travels to a remote island in the Orkneys to build the companion away from his family.
answers.quote: and fixed on one of the remotest of the Orkneys as the scene of my labours.

answers.text: Victor officially breaks his promise to the creature and refuses to build a companion.
answers.quote: “Begone! I do break my promise; never will I create another like yourself, equal in deformity and wickedness.”

answers.text: Victor decides to abandon his island and meet Clerval at Perth.
answers.quote: This letter in a degree recalled me to life, and I determined to quit my island at the expiration of two days.

threads.question: Will the narrator successfully create a female companion, and how will he accomplish it?
threads.raise_quote: Depart to your home, and commence your labours: I shall watch their progress with unutterable anxiety; and fear not but that when you are ready I shall appear.

answers.text: The narrator must return home and begin the work of creating a female companion.
answers.quote: Depart to your home, and commence your labours: I shall watch their progress with unutterable anxiety; and fear not but that when you are ready I shall appear.

answers.text: Victor intends to fulfill his solemn promise to the monster before pursuing any personal happiness.
answers.quote: I must perform my engagement, and let the monster depart with his mate, before I allowed myself to enjoy the delight of an union from which I expected peace.

answers.text: Victor is transporting his chemical instruments to England to begin creating the companion.
answers.quote: I remembered only, and it was with a bitter anguish that I reflected on it, to order that my chemical instruments should be packed to go with me.

answers.text: Victor is beginning the painful process of collecting materials for the female companion in London.
answers.quote: I now also began to collect the materials necessary for my new creation, and this was to me like the torture of single drops of water continually falling on the head.

answers.text: Victor is transporting his chemical instruments from London toward the northern highlands of Scotland to finish his labours.
answers.quote: I packed up my chemical instruments, and the materials I had collected, resolving to finish my labours in some obscure nook in the northern highlands of Scotland.

answers.text: Victor settles in a ruined hut in the Orkneys to perform his work.
answers.quote: On the whole island there were but three miserable huts, and one of these was vacant when I arrived. This I hired.

answers.text: Victor's labor on the female companion is progressing significantly, though it fills him with disgust and dread.
answers.quote: In the meantime I worked on, and my labour was already considerably advanced.

answers.text: Victor destroys the female companion before finishing it and vows never to resume his labours.
answers.quote: I left the room, and, locking the door, made a solemn vow in my own heart never to resume my labours

closed.answer: Victor refuses to complete the female companion and destroys it.
closed.quote: trembling with passion, tore to pieces the thing on which I was engaged.

threads.question: Will the creature truly keep his oath to leave humankind forever once his companion is provided?

answers.text: The creature swears by the sun and sky that he will never be seen again once the companion is given.
The creature's hope is shattered by the destruction of the female companion, inciting his revenge.
answers.quote: with a howl of devilish despair and revenge, withdrew.

threads.question: What is the abhorred task that the narrator has resolved to perform?
threads.raise_quote: and to save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most abhorred task.

answers.text: The abhorred task involves composing a female creature through profound study and laborious disquisition.
answers.quote: I found that I could not compose a female without again devoting several months to profound study and laborious disquisition.

answers.text: The narrator plans to perform the task away from home, in England, to protect his loved ones from horror.
answers.quote: I must absent myself from all I loved while thus employed.

answers.text: Victor's abhorred task is to be completed in a remote hut in the Orkneys.
answers.quote: and fixed on one of the remotest of the Orkneys as the scene of my labours.

answers.text: The abhorred task was the construction of a female creature, which Victor has now destroyed.

closed.answer: The abhorred task was building a second creature, which Victor destroyed out of horror.

threads.question: What is the idea that has struck the narrator's father about the cause of his unhappiness?
Will Clerval discover the narrator's secret undertaking during their journey?
threads.raise_quote: This interfered with the solitude I coveted for the prosecution of my task; yet at the commencement of my journey the presence of my friend could in no way be an impediment, and truly I rejoiced that thus I should be saved many hours of lonely, maddening reflection.

threads.question: Will the creature follow the narrator to England or stay behind and attack his family?

answers.text: The narrator believes the fiend will follow him and exempt his family from danger.
answers.quote: During my absence I should leave my friends unconscious of the existence of their enemy, and unprotected from his attacks, exasperated as he might be by my departure.

answers.text: Victor believes the creature has followed him to the north of Britain.

answers.text: Victor remains in constant terror that his persecutor will appear to claim his companion while he is isolated.

answers.text: Victor is returning to Geneva to protect his family and hunt down the monster.

answers.text: Victor has returned to Geneva and is reunited with Elizabeth.

threads.question: Who is the person in Scotland who invited them to Perth?

threads.question: What specific dark fate or anticipated doom is the narrator referring to when he describes himself as a blasted tree?

answers.quote: But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has entered my soul; and I felt then that I should survive to exhibit, what I shall soon cease to be⁠—a miserable spectacle of wrecked humanity, pitiable to others, and intolerable to myself.

threads.question: What will Victor do in his isolated hut in the Orkneys?

threads.question: What specifically makes the narrator's current labor so horrible and irksome compared to his first experiment?
